title: Dogbert Explains Human Existence Bleakly

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Androids want to be like humans. Tell me what humans do.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Mostly, they eat, sleep, and hope they don't die.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's it?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Unless they find religion... Then they eat, sleep, and look forward to dying.

setting: A living room or sitting room with armchairs
situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert, who is sitting in a large armchair, to describe what humans do, because androids want to imitate them. Dogbert gives a deflating summary of human life, and when Dilbert is disappointed, adds a darker twist about what religious people do.
punchline: Dogbert reduces human existence to eating, sleeping and fearing death, then sardonically suggests that religion merely flips the fear of dying into anticipation of it.
summary: Asked to define humanity for the sake of would-be androids, Dogbert offers a cynical, stripped-down account of daily life and mortality.

title: Wally Provokes Boss With Underwear

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh... Wally, you're wearing only underwear at work.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm trying to get fired.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The company layoff plan is very generous. I'll get a big pile of money if they ask me to leave.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This has given me a degree of freedom in dealing with local management.

setting: Office hallway
situation: Dilbert notices Wally has come to work wearing only his polka-dot underwear, and Wally explains he is trying to get fired so he can collect the company's generous layoff package. As The Boss walks past, Wally, now untroubled by job security, grabs the boss's jacket and pulls it up over his head, using his freedom to bully local management.
punchline: Because Wally wants to be laid off, he has nothing to lose, so he can freely harass his manager without fear of being fired.
summary: Wally strolls into the office in his underwear hoping to be dismissed with a hefty payout, then happily torments his manager since he no longer fears the consequences.

title: Presentations About Having No Presentation

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, do a presentation for the big boss tomorrow morning on the status of your project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There isn't any status. You only assigned the project an hour ago.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well then, do a presentation on why there's no status.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't have time before tomorrow morning.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, then just do a presentation on why there's no time to do a presentation of the status.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And I want to review it two days before you present it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That would be yesterday.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Should I do a presentation on why tomorrow is less than two days from today?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hmm...good. The big boss likes that analytical stuff.

setting: Office cubicle
situation: The Boss orders Dilbert to present on his project's status for the big boss the next morning, even though the project was assigned only an hour ago. Each time Dilbert objects, the Boss simply swaps in a new presentation topic about the obstacle, and then demands a review two days before the presentation. Dilbert points out that deadline already passed and sarcastically proposes yet another meta-presentation, which the Boss enthusiastically accepts.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic suggestion of a presentation on why tomorrow is less than two days away is taken seriously by the Boss, who praises it as analytical, showing management cannot tell absurdity from sincerity.
summary: A manager keeps turning every excuse for not having a presentation into the topic of another presentation, and even mistakes his employee's sarcasm for a good idea.

title: Lunch With a Menacing Executive

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You've been randomly selected to have lunch with a senior executive of the company.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is how the executives show that they are regular people, just like you and me.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: At lunch

transcript.speaker: Senior Executive
transcript.text: I could squash you like a bug!

transcript.speaker: Senior Executive
transcript.text: Ha ha ha ha ha ha!

setting: Office, then a lunch table
situation: Dilbert is told by his boss that he has been randomly picked to lunch with a senior executive, supposedly so the executives can show they are regular people. At the lunch, the unseen executive cheerfully threatens to squash Dilbert like a bug and laughs about it.
punchline: The executive's idea of acting like a regular person is to gleefully threaten an employee, revealing the gulf between management's claimed approachability and their actual attitude.
summary: A staged morale-boosting lunch with an executive turns into a cackling threat against the employee.

title: Hacking the Drug Test Ethically

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's an ethical dilemma... I support my company's goal of discouraging drug use, but the random drug testing policy is a violation of my constitutional rights.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll get fired if I refuse the test. What is the ethical thing to do?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hack into their computer and change your boss's test results.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sometimes the straightest path is through the mud.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Good, rationalize it with an obtuse metaphor.

setting: Dilbert's home, with Dilbert seated in an armchair and later at his computer
situation: Dilbert agonizes over whether to submit to his company's random drug testing, which he feels violates his constitutional rights, and asks Dogbert what the ethical choice is. Dogbert advises hacking into the company computer to change the boss's test results. Dilbert goes along with it, justifying the act with a folksy saying.
punchline: Dogbert's 'ethical' advice is to commit sabotage, and he sarcastically praises Dilbert for covering his dishonest choice with a vague, pretentious metaphor.
summary: Seeking moral guidance on a mandatory drug screening, Dilbert is steered by Dogbert into a dubious hacking scheme that he then excuses with a pat proverb.

title: Dogbert Mocks Ghostwritten Walnut Cookbook

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Book signing today

transcript.speaker: Bobby McNewton
transcript.text: Would you like an autographed copy?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Who are you?

transcript.speaker: Bobby McNewton
transcript.text: I'm Bobby McNewton, child-star from the sixties. I once had a speaking part on "Leave It to Beaver."

transcript.speaker: Bobby McNewton
transcript.text: I'm leveraging my fame to promote my recipe book.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: "Walnuts and milk: Crush walnuts on table. Pour milk on walnuts. Serve cold."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: "Walnuts and pork: Kill a pig. Cook dead pig. Sprinkle walnuts on pig's corpse."

transcript.speaker: Bobby McNewton
transcript.text: I used a ghost writer.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Was he a ghost before he ate your food?

setting: Outside and inside a bookstore during a book signing
situation: Dogbert walks past a bookstore holding a book signing and is offered an autographed copy by Bobby McNewton, a forgotten former child actor. Bobby explains he is using his minor fame to promote his walnut cookbook, and Dogbert reads the absurdly useless recipes aloud. Bobby admits a ghost writer wrote it, prompting Dogbert's insult.
punchline: Dogbert implies the ghost writer died from eating Bobby's terrible recipes, turning "ghost writer" into a literal ghost.
summary: A has-been child star hawks a ridiculous walnut cookbook until a dog reading it suggests the ghost writer was killed by the cooking.

title: Dilbert Mingles With His Boss

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I feel so awkward at these office parties.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've already walked back and forth to the hors d'oeuvres six times.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll stand close to these two and hope they include me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's not working.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll have to find somebody who is alone.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hmm... All the people standing alone look like losers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll just say something... What have I got to lose?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hi.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm Dilbert. What do you do for a living?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm your boss, idiot.

setting: An office party
situation: Dilbert feels awkward at an office party, keeps going back to the food table, and unsuccessfully tries to hover near two coworkers hoping to be included. He decides to approach someone standing alone and introduces himself, asking what the man does for a living.
punchline: The lone person Dilbert picks as a loser to talk to turns out to be his own boss, whom he fails to recognize.
summary: A socially awkward engineer at a company party finally works up the nerve to chat with a stranger, only to discover he's addressing his own manager.
keywords: what do you do for a living

title: Lunch With The Executive Vice President

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How was your lunch with the executive vice president?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Everything was fine until the food fight. He started throwing au gratin potatoes... I countered with an ear of corn to his head and ran for the exit.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When I left, he was face-down in the clam chowder and the kitchen staff was singing "Ding-dong the witch is dead."

setting: Dilbert's home, living room
situation: Dilbert comes home covered in food stains while Dogbert asks how his lunch with the executive vice president went. Dilbert recounts that the lunch erupted into a food fight, that he hit the executive in the head with an ear of corn, and that he fled the restaurant as the executive lay face-down in soup.
punchline: Dilbert, who is normally powerless against upper management, brutally defeats an executive in a food fight, and the restaurant staff celebrate because even they hated the man.
summary: A messy Dilbert reports that a business lunch with a senior executive ended in a food-throwing brawl that he won, to the delight of the kitchen staff.

title: Pink Slip Taken Literally

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My boss gave me the pink slip today.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You must feel pretty bad.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yeah... Pink isn't my color.

setting: Plain lavender background, no specific location (likely Dilbert's home or office)
situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert that his boss gave him the pink slip, meaning he was fired. Dogbert sympathizes, and in the last panel Dilbert is shown wearing a pink slip, the women's undergarment, and complains that the color doesn't suit him.
punchline: Dilbert misinterprets the idiom 'pink slip' (a layoff notice) literally as a pink undergarment, and his concern is about how it looks on him rather than losing his job.
summary: A man told he's been handed his termination notice reacts as if he'd been given a piece of lingerie and worries about the shade.

title: Ratbert Smells of Madonna's Perfume

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Ratbert!

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Dogbert! I've come to visit!

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Your body language says you don't want to hug me. What's wrong? Is it because I'm a rat?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What have you been testing at the lab?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Madonna's "Compulsion" perfume. Why?

setting: A plain room with a pink wall and an electrical outlet
situation: Ratbert arrives to visit Dogbert and happily approaches for a hug, but Dogbert stands stiffly. Ratbert wonders if Dogbert is rejecting him because he's a rat. Dogbert instead asks what Ratbert has been testing at the lab, and Ratbert reveals it's a perfume.
punchline: Dogbert's reluctance isn't prejudice against rats but the smell of the perfume Ratbert was used to test, with the product name 'Compulsion' hinting that Dogbert is struggling with an urge to hug him.
summary: A friendly lab rat is puzzled by a cool reception until it emerges that he reeks of the fragrance he's been guinea-pigging.

title: English Teacher Hiccups Grammar Joke

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Up I hicc!

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Up I hicc!

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Up I hicc! Up I hicc!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: (thought) English teacher.

setting: A park bench outdoors
situation: A woman with glasses sits on a park bench next to Dogbert and keeps making a strange 'up I hicc' sound. Dogbert, wearing glasses, listens and figures out what is going on.
punchline: The woman is an English teacher whose hiccups come out grammatically correct, as 'hic-up' reversed into 'up I hicc', and Dogbert deduces her profession from it.
summary: A bench neighbor's odd repeated noise turns out to be the telltale quirk of someone who teaches grammar for a living.

title: Despot Escapes Garden Festival Mob

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: A mob of Elbonians is at the gate!! They have pickaxes and rakes!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Quick!! We'll take the emergency despot escape slingshot!!

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Did anybody remind the king that today is the Garden Festival?

setting: A medieval-style castle in Elbonia, with a throne and a stone staircase
situation: Dilbert warns Dogbert, who sits on a throne as the despot king, that a mob of Elbonians with pickaxes and rakes is at the gate. Dilbert hurries him up the castle steps to the emergency despot escape slingshot and launches him away. In the final panel the crowd, in black hoods and carrying garden tools, wonders whether anyone told the king it was Garden Festival day.
punchline: The supposedly angry mob was just a crowd of villagers with gardening tools arriving for a harmless festival, so the king fled and was launched needlessly.
summary: A panicked royal flight from an apparent armed mob turns out to be a misunderstanding about a gardening holiday.

title: Dogbert Reviews Dilbert in Newspaper

transcript.text: I've become a newspaper critic.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I criticize ordinary people... I started with you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey, here it is...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's this little symbol mean?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's a dog sniffing himself... it's like getting one star.

setting: Dilbert's living room, with Dilbert in an armchair reading a newspaper
situation: Dogbert announces he has become a newspaper critic who reviews ordinary people, and says he started with Dilbert. Dilbert finds the review in the paper and asks what a little symbol next to it means. Dogbert explains it is a dog sniffing himself, his equivalent of a one-star rating.
punchline: Dogbert's rating symbol for Dilbert is a dog sniffing himself, an insulting stand-in for a one-star review, showing Dilbert got the worst possible score.
summary: A dog turned newspaper reviewer of everyday folks gives his own owner the lowest possible mark using a crude canine icon.

title: Physics Made Easy: Time and Donuts

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Physics made easy

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Today's lesson is "time."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Imagine a donut, fired from a cannon at the speed of light while rotating.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Time is like that, except without the cannon and the donut.

setting: A classroom or lecture area with a whiteboard, under the heading 'Physics Made Easy'
situation: Dilbert gives a physics lesson on the concept of time. He asks the audience to imagine a spinning donut fired from a cannon at light speed, illustrated on a whiteboard diagram. He then says time is like that, minus the cannon and the donut.
punchline: The 'explanation' strips away every element of the analogy, leaving nothing, so it explains nothing and the lesson is not 'easy' at all.
summary: A lecturer pretends to demystify time with an absurd flying-pastry analogy and then removes all the parts of it.

title: Dogbert Annoys Dilbert Over Ears

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm in a bad mood. I'll have to annoy Dilbert and see if it makes me feel better.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I just noticed that your ears don't match from the back.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gasp!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Ahh...

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: Dogbert, in a bad mood, decides to cheer himself up by annoying Dilbert. He walks up to Dilbert at his computer and says his ears don't match from behind. Dilbert gasps and clutches his ears in horror while Dogbert contentedly enjoys the result.
punchline: Dogbert deliberately plants a baseless insecurity in Dilbert purely to improve his own mood, and it works instantly.
summary: A grumpy Dogbert tests whether tormenting Dilbert with a made-up flaw about his ears will lift his spirits, and it does.

title: Therapist Blames Mother Under Couch

transcript.speaker: Therapist
transcript.text: Your problem is my mother.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your mother? I don't even know your mother. How could she be my problem?

transcript.speaker: Therapist
transcript.text: She's an evil woman and she lives under the couch.

transcript.speaker: Therapist's Mother
transcript.text: What you need is a good swat!

setting: Therapist's office
situation: Dilbert lies on a therapy couch while his therapist, notepad in hand, announces that his problem is her own mother. When Dilbert objects that he doesn't even know her mother, the therapist explains that the mother is an evil woman who lives under the couch. An elderly woman then pops up brandishing a rolled-up newspaper and threatens Dilbert with a swat.
punchline: The therapist reverses the usual blame-your-mother script by projecting her own problem onto the patient, and the 'evil' mother literally lurks under the couch ready to hit him.
summary: A role-reversed therapy session turns absurd when the counselor's own mother ambushes the patient from beneath the furniture.

title: Annual Vacation Nobody Enjoys

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We have completed our obligation to take a vacation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: As usual, we hated every minute of it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why do we do it every year?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My theory is that you're stupid.

setting: Dilbert's front doorway and then his living room
situation: Dilbert walks back in his front door with a backpack, announcing that he has fulfilled his duty to take a vacation and that he hated every minute of it. Settled in his armchair with a snack, he asks Dogbert why they repeat the experience every year. Dogbert, also eating, replies that the reason is Dilbert's stupidity.
punchline: Dogbert bluntly explains that people keep doing miserable vacations every year simply because they're stupid.
summary: After another joyless holiday, Dilbert wonders why he keeps taking them, and Dogbert delivers a blunt diagnosis.

title: No Smart Person Works Here

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why should I hire you as my business consultant?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I have credibility because I don't work for your company. No smart person would work here full-time.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I work here full-time.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Sorry. I'll try to speak slower.

setting: The Boss's office
situation: Dogbert interviews to be the Boss's business consultant, and the Boss asks why he should be hired. Dogbert says his credibility comes from not working for the company, since no smart person would work there full-time. When the Boss objects that he works there full-time, Dogbert apologizes and offers to speak more slowly.
punchline: Dogbert insults the Boss's intelligence by implying that, as a full-time employee, he is not smart enough to follow the explanation.
summary: A dog pitching himself as a consultant insults the company, then condescendingly offers to slow down when his prospective client takes offense.

title: Dogbert Cheats With Armed Queen

transcript.speaker: Dogbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You did the same thing when we played Scrabble.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert

setting: A table where Dilbert and Dogbert play chess
situation: Dilbert is confident as he captures a rook in a chess game with Dogbert. Dogbert responds by announcing that his queen has an Uzi and wipes out all of Dilbert's pieces, knocking them over. Dilbert complains that Dogbert pulled the same trick in Scrabble, and Dogbert tells him to take it like a man.
punchline: Dogbert ignores the rules of the game by inventing absurd, violent powers for his pieces, then dismisses Dilbert's complaint as a lack of manliness.
summary: A chess game collapses when Dogbert declares that his queen is carrying a machine gun and refuses to accept any objections.

title: Dilbert's Free Energy Schemes

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: How to get free energy

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The world is full of free energy, if you know where to look.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: For example, the phone company sends extra electricity to make your phone ring.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You can plug your phone line into a big rechargeable battery...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then give suckers a reason to call.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And what about junk mail? Are you just throwing it away?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you know it can be burned to heat your house?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Next week I'll tell you how to get electricity from your houseguests.

setting: Dilbert's home and street, presented like an instructional how-to segment
situation: Dilbert gives a tongue-in-cheek tutorial on harvesting free energy. He suggests wiring a phone line to a giant battery and posting 'Free Money? Call' flyers to trick people into phoning, then burning junk mail to heat the house. He ends by teasing a future lesson on extracting electricity from houseguests.
punchline: His free-energy tips are really schemes to drain power from unsuspecting people, and the closing teaser implies he plans to do the same to his guests.
summary: A scheming Dilbert lectures on cheap power tricks that mostly involve exploiting gullible callers, burning unwanted mail, and eventually shocking visitors.

title: Recognizing an Employee Who Quit

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Thanks, but I'm not Wilson. He quit months ago.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've got to stop calling this the Employee Recognition Program.

setting: Office meeting room during a staff gathering
situation: The Boss addresses a group of employees and praises Wilson for working twenty-hour days to make a project succeed. A man steps forward to say he isn't Wilson, who left months ago. The Boss, embarrassed, thinks to himself that the program shouldn't be called employee recognition.
punchline: The Boss's recognition program is so detached from reality that he can't even identify the people he's honoring, so the name 'Employee Recognition Program' is a lie.
summary: A manager's attempt to publicly honor a hard-working staffer falls apart when he singles out the wrong person, revealing he never knew the man had left.

A flight attendant then tells Dilbert to put his carry-on luggage in the overhead compartment, implying Dogbert has been treated as luggage.
punchline: Dogbert is angry about the flight arrangements because he's being treated as Dilbert's carry-on luggage, and the flight attendant's request to stow him overhead confirms it.
summary: A pet dog traveling with his owner on a plane growls through the flight until a stewardess asks that the owner's carry-on be put up in the bin.

setting: A park bench outdoors on a grassy hill
situation: A muscular man in a sleeveless outfit sits on a park bench next to Dogbert and complains that being a professional bodybuilder is hard because he sounds dumb when he explains his job at parties. Dogbert asks how the pay is, and the bodybuilder is puzzled by the question.
punchline: The bodybuilder worries only about sounding dumb and has no idea that a job is supposed to pay money, which shows he really is dim.
summary: A buff man frets about how his job sounds at parties, then reveals he doesn't even grasp the idea of being paid for it.

punchline: The attendants find emptying their minds effortless because they have almost no thoughts to begin with, a jab at the intelligence of people in dead-end jobs.
summary: Told to blank their minds in a relaxation lesson, a roomful of trainee attendants finds the task laughably simple.

punchline: The boss's secretary is such an intimidating gatekeeper that approaching her feels like facing a mythical guardian, and Dilbert responds by comparing the ordeal to the Wizard of Oz's terrifying winged monkeys.
summary: Getting an appointment with the boss means braving a fearsome secretary who treats scheduling like a deadly trial straight out of a fantasy movie.

title: Elbonia's National Bird Is Frisbee

transcript.speaker: Dogbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Condor?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Frisbee.

setting: Dilbert's home, with Dogbert sitting in an armchair
situation: Dilbert argues that the people of Elbonia are simple but capable of handling democracy. Dogbert, wearing a crown, asks if Dilbert knows Elbonia's national bird. Dilbert guesses condor, and Dogbert answers that it is a frisbee.
punchline: Elbonians are so simple-minded that they think a frisbee is a bird, which undercuts Dilbert's claim that they can handle democracy.
summary: Dilbert defends the intellectual capacity of a backward nation until Dogbert's bird quiz exposes how primitive its people really are.

title: Child Costs Equal Buying Norway

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My program predicts that the cost of college will rise twenty percent a year...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now, throw in the cost of orthodontia and haircuts...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can either have a child or buy Norway...

setting: Dilbert's home computer room
situation: Dilbert sits at his computer running a financial projection program on the future cost of raising a child. He adds college tuition increases, then orthodontia and haircuts. In the last panel he holds a long printout and concludes the total is comparable to buying an entire country.
punchline: The projected expense of raising a child is so enormous that it equals the price of purchasing the nation of Norway.
summary: After feeding mounting child-rearing expenses into his computer, Dilbert is left staring at a printout so huge that parenthood looks like an alternative to owning a whole country.

title: Dilbert Lifts Weights for Armpits

transcript.text: Notice anything different?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're holding your arms out like this.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've been lifting weights!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My arms do this automatically because of the muscles.

setting: Dilbert's home or office, with a wooden desk in the background
situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert if he notices anything different, and Dogbert points out that Dilbert is holding his arms out stiffly. Dilbert explains he has been lifting weights and that bulging armpit muscles now force his arms outward. He vows to keep going until his armpits are so huge his arms must point straight up, all in the name of looking good.
punchline: Dilbert's absurd vanity leads him to pursue grotesquely oversized armpit muscles, mistaking an awkward side effect of weightlifting for an attractive result.
summary: A man proudly shows off his new gym-built physique, which consists mainly of arms that can no longer hang normally.

title: Pulling Excalibert From the Sharpener

transcript.text: Somebody left a pencil in the electric sharpener.

transcript.speaker: Co-worker
transcript.text: That's "Excalibert."

transcript.speaker: Co-worker
transcript.text: Legend has it that whoever can remove Excalibert from the sharpener will become CEO.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Like this?

transcript.speaker: Narrator

setting: Office cubicle with an electric pencil sharpener on a desk
situation: Dilbert notices a pencil stuck in an electric sharpener, and a co-worker explains it is called "Excalibert" and that whoever pulls it out will become CEO. Dilbert casually yanks the pencil free, triggering a burst of light and a beam shooting upward, while the stunned co-worker looks on. The strip ends with a "continued" tag.
punchline: The office parody of the Excalibur legend plays out literally when Dilbert, without ceremony, pulls the pencil out and fulfils the prophecy of becoming CEO.
summary: A jammed pencil becomes office mythology, and the one person who nonchalantly frees it unleashes a dazzling flash of destiny.

title: Dogbert Denies Everything at Senate Hearing

transcript.speaker: Dogbert

transcript.speaker: Senator
transcript.text: We're not accusing you...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hey, I didn't bring it up!

setting: Senate Judiciary Committee hearing room
situation: Dogbert sits alone at a witness table facing a panel of senators at a confirmation-style hearing. When asked a routine legal question about how he would interpret Roe versus Wade, he reflexively declares the accusers are lying and denies everything. The senators say they are not accusing him, and Dogbert insists he was not the one who raised the subject.
punchline: Dogbert responds to a neutral legal question as if he were guilty of something, with reflexive denial and blame-shifting that makes him sound far more suspect than if he had simply answered.
summary: A witness before a legislative panel treats a simple legal question as an accusation and defensively denies wrongdoing nobody alleged.

title: Male Bonding Through Cruel Insults

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

characters: Coworker with glasses and bald head
setting: Office break area
situation: A coworker named Brad insults Dilbert and another bald coworker as 'ugly people' and 'cow pies', claiming it is just male bonding. When Dilbert tries the same approach, he insults Brad by revealing that Bruce is seeing Brad's wife and that his children are funny looking. Brad reacts with a violent outburst while Dilbert reflects that insulting people actually felt good.
punchline: Dilbert discovers that Brad's 'male bonding' of cruel insults is really just a licence to be cruel, and it feels satisfying when he does it back, with far worse results.
summary: A bully excuses his insults as friendly bonding, so Dilbert returns the favor with brutal personal jabs and finds he enjoys it.

title: Perpetual Motion Needs Spare Time

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm obsessed with inventing a perpetual motion device.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Most scientists think it's impossible, but I have something they don't.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: A lot of spare time?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Exactly.

setting: Dilbert's home or workspace, at a desk
situation: Dilbert tinkers with a green gadget at his desk while telling Dogbert he is obsessed with building a perpetual motion machine. He boasts that he has an advantage over scientists who call it impossible. Dogbert guesses that the advantage is plenty of free time, and Dilbert cheerfully agrees.
punchline: Dilbert's only edge over the scientists is that he has no social life or other obligations, which Dogbert deadpans and Dilbert happily admits.
summary: An engineer pursuing an impossible invention reveals that his sole qualification is having nothing else to do.

title: Selling Ceramic Nose Puppies

setting: A city sidewalk beside a vendor's cart
situation: A street vendor hawks "nose puppies" from a cart priced at $1.00 each. Dilbert asks what they are, and the vendor explains they are tiny ceramic puppies that fit inside your nose. The vendor then proudly cites the business motto "find a need and fill it."
punchline: The vendor's motto about meeting customer needs is absurd because nobody has a need for a ceramic puppy in their nose, mocking entrepreneurial clichés and pointless products.
summary: A cart vendor peddles pointless nose-sized ceramic dogs while claiming to be serving a genuine market demand.
keywords: find a need and fill it

title: Anti-Gravity Formula Seeks Attention

transcript.text: Notice anything?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert

setting: Dilbert's home laboratory
situation: Dilbert excitedly discovers that his anti-gravity formula makes a test tube float, and imagines the fame and praise he will receive after drinking it. In the last panel he hovers horizontally in mid-air and asks Dogbert if he notices anything, while Dogbert lies on the floor unimpressed.
punchline: Dogbert ignores the scientific miracle of a flying man and dismisses it as Dilbert's desperate need for attention, undercutting his dream of praise and admiration.
summary: A scientist floats in the air after testing his gravity-defying potion, only to have his pet brush off the feat as a cry for attention.

title: Paper or Plastic Guilt Trip

transcript.speaker: Grocery Clerk

transcript.text: Paper that can be recycled ... or an evil, selfish, short-sighted, planet-destroying, stupid plastic bag?!!

transcript.speaker: Grocery Clerk
transcript.text: Good. That's all we have.

setting: Grocery store checkout counter
situation: A grocery clerk asks Dilbert whether he wants a paper or plastic bag, then loads the question with an angry rant about how destructive plastic bags are. Dilbert calmly chooses plastic anyway. The clerk replies that this is fine because plastic is all the store has.
punchline: The clerk pretends to offer a choice and guilt-trips the customer toward paper, even though the store only stocks plastic bags, so the choice was never real.
summary: A cashier bullies a shopper over his bag options only to admit that one of them doesn't even exist.

title: Doctor Summons Demon to Heal Arm

transcript.speaker: Doctor

setting: Doctor's examination room
situation: Dilbert sits on an exam table holding his injured arm while the doctor proposes an unconventional treatment. The doctor then raises his arms and chants an incantation to a demon. When Dilbert asks if this has ever worked, the doctor admits he has never tried it before, as a demon's clawed hand reaches into the frame.
punchline: The doctor is experimenting on his patient with a demonic ritual and cheerfully admits he has no idea whether it works because he has never tried it.
summary: A physician chants to a demon to fix a patient's arm, then confesses the method is completely untested.

title: Vacation Money Down a Hole

setting: A barren canyon or crater on vacation, with Dilbert and Dogbert standing at the edge of a hole
situation: Dilbert and Dogbert are at their vacation destination, Clyde Canyon, which appears to be nothing more than a hole in the ground. Dilbert admits he should have asked more questions before booking, then struggles to find a metaphor for wasted money, and Dogbert supplies the answer.
punchline: Dilbert tries to reassure himself that his vacation money isn't being wasted, but Dogbert points out that the vacation is literally a hole in the ground, which Dilbert grudgingly confirms.
summary: A man who booked a trip without doing his homework discovers his destination is nothing but a literal pit.

title: Engineer Defeated by VCR Instructions

setting: Dilbert's home, in front of a new VCR and TV
situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert to read the VCR instructions aloud while he connects the cables. The technical jargon baffles Dilbert, an electrical engineer, who decides he'll hide his confusion from his colleagues. Dogbert then reads fake instructions telling Dilbert to strip naked, cover himself in motor oil and run through town, and Dilbert asks to see the page.
punchline: Dogbert makes up absurd instructions, including one telling Dilbert not to doubt him, to prey on Dilbert's confusion with the incomprehensible manual.
summary: A baffled engineer lets his dog read the VCR manual, and the dog slips in ridiculous made-up steps that the confused man almost believes.

title: CEO Offer Means Employee Layoffs

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I accept, what will I say to the employees?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How about "neener neener"?

setting: Executive office
situation: An executive tells Dilbert that a Japanese firm has offered to buy the company. Dilbert would become CEO and earn $68 million, but every employee would be laid off. Dilbert asks what he would tell the employees, and Dogbert suggests taunting them.
punchline: Dogbert's advice to answer mass layoffs with a childish "neener neener" mocks how callous executives are toward the workers they cash out on.
summary: Offered a fortune to run a company whose staff would all be fired, Dilbert seeks a message for them and gets a schoolyard taunt from his dog.

title: Tiny Coworker Challenges Meeting to Fight

setting: Conference room during a meeting
situation: At a meeting, a small, bald, bespectacled man at the table loudly announces he disagrees with everything and challenges everyone to a fight, boasting he can beat anyone despite his size. A woman across the table joins in with her own challenge to fight. A coworker then explains that the aggression is her fault because she accidentally used him to mop up a coffee spill.
punchline: The coworker's explanation that she used the angry little man as a sponge for spilled coffee absurdly treats him like an object and implies his bad mood is a result of that indignity.
summary: A pint-sized attendee picks a fight with a whole conference room, and the odd reason for his temper turns out to involve a coffee mishap and a very unusual cleanup tool.

title: Untrained Doctors at Jiffy Med Center

setting: Examination room at the Jiffy Med Center
situation: Dilbert sits on an exam table while a doctor in a white coat with a stethoscope explains how the clinic keeps health costs low. He admits that no staff have any medical training, which is why they are paid almost nothing. When Dilbert asks why he does the job, the doctor cheerfully says he enjoys putting the cold stethoscope on naked people.
punchline: The unqualified clinic worker has no interest in medicine and is only in it for the creepy thrill of pressing a stethoscope on naked patients.
summary: A cut-rate clinic brags about cheap care from untrained staff, and its fake doctor reveals a disturbing motive for doing the job.

punchline: The scientists' idea of a bake sale entry is an elaborate model volcano, so the competition stays absurdly nerdy, with Dilbert joking that his volcano is so realistic it terrifies the local population.
summary: Scientists take their charity bake sale so seriously that the entries turn into science-fair volcanoes.

punchline: The sheep deliver a string of deliberately terrible puns (herding, mutton for punishment, sheepless nights), making the strip itself a gag about sheep jokes.
summary: A shepherd leads his flock across a meadow while the sheep amuse themselves with a chain of bad wordplay.

title: Dogbert and the Necktie Snake

situation: Dogbert approaches a garbage man hauling a trash can and asks why Dilbert's neckties curl up. The garbage man offers a deadpan, elaborate explanation about a Tanzanian necktie snake that disguises itself and stalks people for years. He dramatizes the attack by clutching his own throat and choking.
punchline: The garbage man confidently supplies an absurd, made-up answer to a trivial question and acts out the snake attack, showing he'll play along with any nonsense.
summary: Asked about a puzzling wardrobe quirk, a trash collector spins a wild tale about a disguised, patient serpent and melodramatically demonstrates its strike.

title: Salespeople Swarm When Just Browsing

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

setting: A retail store with a sale sign
situation: Dilbert stands in a store thinking about how much he hates shopping, complaining in his thoughts that no salesperson is ever available when he actually wants to buy something. In the last panel, several salespeople pile onto him, grabbing and clinging to him, the moment he is only browsing.
punchline: Salespeople are absent when you need help buying but aggressively swarm you when you just want to look around.
summary: A reluctant shopper laments missing clerks, then gets mobbed by a pack of them as soon as he's merely browsing.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And dogs are better than people.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But people are better than cats.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And cats are evil...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Therefore, all people are stupid.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't follow that logic.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yes, my theory predicts you would say that.

setting: Outdoors on a walking path, then under a large tree
situation: Dilbert takes a walk with Dogbert and asks whether people are basically good or evil. Dogbert ranks dogs, people and cats in a chain of comparisons and concludes that all people are stupid. When Dilbert says he doesn't follow the logic, Dogbert says that is exactly what his theory predicted.
punchline: Dogbert's theory is unfalsifiable: Dilbert's objection to the flawed logic is treated as proof that people are stupid, so any response confirms it.
summary: A walk in the park turns into a flimsy ranking of dogs, people and cats that ends with a self-confirming claim of human stupidity.

situation: The Boss is chatting about fish with a coworker, gesturing broadly with his arm, then greets Dilbert with the same outstretched arm. Dilbert misreads the gesture as a hug invitation and embraces the Boss. To avoid awkwardness he then also hugs the stranger standing nearby, who looks horrified.
punchline: Dilbert's attempt to be a modern, affectionate 'nineties guy' results in him hugging two bewildered men who never asked for it, undercutting his smug claim of having outgrown the uptight eighties.
summary: A misread arm gesture leads Dilbert to hug his boss and then a total stranger, all in the name of being modern.

summary: A dinosaur's innocent curiosity about political dishonesty ends in a screaming fit once the dog explains how elections really work.

Wally says he made exactly one: he covered his cubicle in sticky notes and turned it into a tourist attraction meant to bring in revenue. The final panel shows the sprawling sticky-note structure, which has attracted few visitors.
punchline: Given empowerment with no real guidance or authority, Wally used it on a ridiculous, useless project, and it isn't even making money.
summary: After his boss grants everyone empowerment, Wally uses his new decision-making freedom to convert his workspace into a sticky-note tourist trap that nobody visits.

situation: Dilbert proudly shows off his new optical disk (CD-ROM) player and boasts that he can now instantly look up Shakespeare or Greek history. Dogbert asks how often he actually needs to do that, and when Dilbert accuses him of not understanding technology, Dogbert replies that he is just a dog.
punchline: Dogbert's deadpan question exposes that Dilbert bought the gadget for capabilities he has no real need for, and his 'I'm just a dog' reply sarcastically dodges the accusation while implying the criticism still stands.
summary: A man excited about his new computer accessory is gently deflated by his dog's practical question about whether he'll ever really use it.

summary: Lunch companions compete with outrageous sickness tales until one launches into a tedious home repair anecdote that proves the most unbearable of all.

situation: A man in a yellow shirt stops to ask Ratbert, who is wearing a turtleneck sweater, whether he is a Chihuahua. summary: A rat dressed in a sweater passes as a small dog because the man questioning him quickly forgets to wonder whether he's right.

summary: A self-assured engineer pretends to repair a stranger's dead car, only for her to call him a fraud and point out she is simply out of fuel.

title: Elbonians Demand Free Speech, Mock Hat

summary: Subjects insist on freedom of expression while admitting that social conformity will prevent any new ideas and that they mainly want to tease their ruler's headwear.

title: Dogbert's D.B. Cooper Museum Exhibit

setting: Dogbert's museum, in front of a curtained exhibit
situation: Dogbert, acting as a museum curator, shows a couple of visitors an exhibit hidden behind a curtain. He explains the D.B. Cooper hijacking story, then pulls back the curtain to reveal a grisly display of boots, a bag and wreckage.
punchline: Cooper's parachute failed because the airline he robbed supplied it, implying they sabotaged it, and the remains in the display prove it.
summary: A canine curator unveils the gruesome fate of a famous skyjacker whose stolen-ransom getaway went fatally wrong.

situation: Dilbert flips through his high school yearbook with Dogbert and reminisces about a classmate he and others used to torment by tying him to the flagpole and stuffing live frogs in his pants. punchline: The boy Dilbert bullied now runs the school, and his unhappiness is presented as a mystery rather than an obvious result of the abuse he suffered there.
summary: A man fondly recalling the schoolmate he used to torture learns, and shrugs off, that the victim never left the school and never recovered his cheer.

title: Hostile Takeover Bravado, Clothes Chewed Off

punchline: His tough talk about being a formidable adversary collapses when the acquirer's lawyers literally strip him of everything, showing how outmatched he really was.
summary: After boldly refusing a buyout offer, a man returns humiliated and half-clothed after facing the opposing legal team.

punchline: Dilbert's sneeze is so powerful it devastates the meeting, and his only responses are denial or fleeing and assuming a new identity.
summary: A sneeze of absurd force wrecks a meeting room and leaves the sneezer contemplating a fresh start under a false name.

summary: A tour guide dog presents a supposedly priceless silk shirt, but a visitor sees only a cheap polyester shirt, prompting a smug quip about the gift shop.

punchline: Even a world-changing scientific breakthrough floating right above their heads can't compete with the coworkers' mundane small talk, which they don't even notice him interrupting.
summary: A man who has defied gravity hovers over his colleagues, who remain absorbed in comparing their trivial weekend hobbies.

summary: Two friends dutifully return a lost wallet to a self-declared criminal and end up being robbed at gunpoint for their trouble.

summary: A canine headmaster trains uniformed students in the art of idly sitting in a booth and promises the talent will carry over to politics or photo kiosks.

punchline: Ratbert asks for a short farewell but can't help launching into a sentimental speech, and when Dogbert takes him at his word and leaves, Ratbert saves face by pretending that's what he wanted.
summary: A little lab rat requests a brief farewell, immediately contradicts himself with a flowery tribute, and is left stranded when his friend simply leaves.

situation: Dogbert compliments Ratbert on his Chihuahua disguise, then insists he must also learn to think like one. He tells Ratbert to contemplate the sound of one hand clapping, a Zen riddle. Ratbert strains his mind, yelps that he has sprained his brain, and starts yipping like a Chihuahua.

summary: A Zen puzzle fries a rat's brain until he is yapping like the small nervous dog he is pretending to be.

title: Dogbert Enjoys Lying As Salesman

setting: Dilbert's living room, then a used car lot
situation: Dogbert tells Dilbert he has become a used car salesman, and explains he does it not for the pay but because he likes lying to strangers. On the car lot, Dogbert pitches a car to a customer, and instead of lying he gives a candid description that accidentally reveals it was owned by a diamond smuggler.
punchline: Dogbert claims to love lying to customers, but his sales pitch is so brutally honest, accidentally exposing the car's criminal history, that it shows he is terrible at the job.
summary: A dog who brags that he loves deceiving strangers ends up undermining his own used car sale by revealing the vehicle's shady smuggling past.

title: Lemons, Allergies, and Swelling Up

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You know what they say, "If life gives you lemons, swell up and die."

setting: Outdoors on a rocky outcrop under a blue sky
situation: Dilbert sits on a rock and complains that he has no luck. Dogbert offers the standard proverb about turning lemons into lemonade. Dilbert points out he is allergic to citrus, and Dogbert coldly revises the proverb to say he should swell up and die.
punchline: Dogbert twists the optimistic lemonade proverb into a deadpan, unsympathetic suggestion that Dilbert should simply die from his allergy.
summary: A friend's cheery proverb about making the best of bad luck collapses when an allergy makes it useless, and the dog replaces it with a grim alternative.

He admits that every member is male because they all joined to meet women, and asks for ideas. One member suggests merging with the Aerobic Instructor Anti-Defamation League.
punchline: The members' only idea for fixing the group's gender imbalance is to merge with a club of aerobic instructors, which shows they still just want to meet women.
summary: A club of men formed to fight a stereotype is made up entirely of men who joined for dating, and their proposed fix is to pair up with a group of fitness instructors.

title: Empowerment Means Firing Each Other

situation: The Boss announces that all employees are now empowered to make their own decisions, promising they'll be happier and more productive. Immediately, Wally uses his new power to fire Dilbert, Dilbert fires him right back, and Alice declares she'll never work hard again.
punchline: Given real decision-making power, employees use it for petty or lazy ends, such as firing each other and slacking off, showing the boss's empowerment fad backfires.
summary: A manager hands his staff newfound authority and watches them promptly misuse it on firings and a vow of laziness.

setting: Dilbert's home, at a makeshift sculpting workspace
situation: Dilbert holds a mallet and chisel and explains that sculpting an elephant is supposedly easy: just chip away everything that doesn't look like an elephant. Dogbert watches from a stool. Later, the block has been reduced to a pile of rubble on the stand, and Dilbert concludes the marble must not have had an elephant in it.
punchline: Dilbert blames the material rather than his own lack of skill, after reducing the entire block to rubble by following oversimplified instructions.
summary: After following a glib recipe for carving an elephant, a man reduces his marble block to gravel and decides the stone was simply defective.

situation: Dilbert drives down a road while narrating his growing curiosity about something lying ahead, which he first guesses is a squished animal. He admits he doesn't want to look but can't resist, then is horrified, only to discover it's just an old shoe. Moments later he spots another small blob in the road and Dogbert, riding beside him, says it's his brain.
punchline: Dogbert implies that Dilbert's brain has fallen out of his head, mocking his panicky, overwrought reaction to a harmless old shoe.
summary: A driver works himself into a panic over an object in the road that turns out to be a shoe, and his canine passenger then quips that the next speck on the pavement is the driver's missing brain.

situation: Dogbert, working as a consultant, presents a flip chart to a boss and a woman executive, telling them their profits are plunging. His next chart compares brainpower, showing competitors with a huge brain, beavers with a small one, and the client's company with a tiny dot. Oblivious, the boss asks whether they should cut the training budget again.
punchline: Dogbert's chart shows the company has less brainpower than beavers, and the boss proves it by proposing to cut training yet again, the very thing that created the problem.
summary: A consultant dog charts his clients' intelligence as smaller than a beaver's, and they respond with a plan that confirms it.

punchline: Floyd is depicted as a literal parasite on a colleague's back, so getting rid of him is like lancing a boil, and Dilbert's only concern is whether it leaves a hickey-like mark.
summary: A worn-out colleague warns that the freeloader attached to Dilbert's back can be removed like a boil, though the cure may leave a mark.

situation: Dilbert shows Dogbert a machine he invented that automatically pets him. Dogbert dismisses it as Dilbert's dumbest idea while the device pats his head. Dilbert points out that Dogbert is clearly enjoying it.
punchline: Dogbert insults the invention but is visibly enjoying the petting, and his demand to be left alone proves Dilbert right.
summary: A robotic head-patting gadget gets scorned by the dog it was built for, yet he happily keeps using it.

title: Dilbert's Homemade Superhero Suit

setting: Dilbert's home
situation: Dilbert shows Dogbert a superhero costume he sewed, explaining that he might accidentally gain super powers someday. He then puts it on, a blue cowl, red cape and a large 'D' on the chest, and says it will keep his identity secret. Dogbert deadpans that he now understands why secrecy matters.
punchline: Dogbert's remark implies that anyone seeing Dilbert in such a ridiculous costume would want to keep their identity secret out of embarrassment, not for heroism.
summary: A man in a homemade caped costume with his own initial on it hopes it will hide who he is, and his dog finds a different reason to want anonymity.

Only a small rat-like creature, Ratbert, is nearby listening. Dogbert then explains that it was just practice, while Ratbert complains his eyes are stuck in a zombie-like stare.
punchline: Dogbert's grand speech to the 'masses' was rehearsed for an audience of one, and Ratbert's zombie-eyed stare shows he was mindlessly entranced by the performance.
summary: A dog rehearses his world-domination speech on a hilltop, and his only audience is a small creature left in a hypnotized daze.

title: Dogbert's Invisible People Blame Theory

punchline: Dogbert applies his own theory immediately, blaming imaginary people named Juan and Cindy for the criticism, showing how absurdly convenient blame-shifting is.
summary: A self-appointed canine guru preaches that invisible people cause everyone's troubles, then promptly pins a complaint on two of them.

situation: Dilbert sits at his desk drawing and claims that sketching The Simpsons is easy. He proudly shows Dogbert a drawing of Bart riding a bicycle. Dogbert, unimpressed, critiques the drawing.

summary: After boasting about how simple a certain cartoon family is to sketch, a man shows off his amateur doodle and gets a blunt critique from his dog.

title: CEO Pay Versus Staff Cuts

Dilbert asks whether the CEO was just paid twenty million dollars, and the Boss admits it, justifying it by saying risky jobs deserve higher pay. Dilbert points out that it is the employees, not the CEO, whose jobs are actually at risk.
punchline: The Boss defends the CEO's enormous pay as compensation for a risky job, when it is the rank-and-file staff who are actually facing layoffs.
summary: Staff question why layoffs are needed when the CEO just earned a fortune, and the justification offered collapses because the real risk falls on the workers.

Dilbert muses about the optimist's half-full or half-empty question, and Dogbert offers a sarcastic answer. Dilbert then cheerfully proposes setting up a base camp in the tiny crevice.
punchline: The canyon is so small that it is a ridiculous hole in the ground, which Dogbert dismisses as 'half baked' (poorly conceived), while Dilbert absurdly plans a base camp for an expedition into a tiny dent.
summary: A disappointing tourist attraction turns out to be a puny ditch, prompting a snarky pun and a mock expedition plan.

He demonstrates how it was staged with foil-wrapped Barbie dolls and a globe, then acts out the doll astronauts' dialogue with melodramatic cries for help. Dogbert dryly comments on the quality of the script.
punchline: Dogbert sarcastically implies that the cheesy, melodramatic dialogue Lucas just performed must have been written by someone else, since Lucas is famously criticized for weak dialogue in his films.
summary: A famous filmmaker brags that he secretly staged the lunar landing with dolls, and his dog mocks the hammy script he performs.

summary: A violent-minded man flunks Dogbert's friend-matching quiz and is left with dismal options, yet he ends up making a friend through a random shared grudge.

summary: A man stuck on a crossword clue is insulted by his dog, whose insult turns out to be the exact word he needs.

summary: A man groggy from sleeping late decides the remedy for his sleep-induced headache is to crawl back under the blankets.
