He explains his guilt-elimination method by claiming that all of their problems are caused by invisible people named Juan and Cindy. He then concludes that the audience simply needs to find and kill them.
punchline: Dogbert's self-help advice is absurd and sinister: he invents imaginary scapegoats to blame for everything, then tells people to murder them, mocking self-help gurus who encourage people to blame others rather than take responsibility.
summary: A scheming dog on a lecture stage tells his audience to cure their guilt by hunting down the imaginary culprits behind all their troubles.

title: Boss Blames Computer For Positive Drug Tests

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm discontinuing the employee drug testing program...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Because my own tests keep turning out positive... which makes me suspect that some wiseguy has tampered with the medical computer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Denial and paranoia... classic symptoms.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Is he "high" right now?

setting: Office meeting room
situation: The Boss tells his staff he is cancelling the employee drug testing program because his own test results keep coming back positive. He assumes someone has tampered with the medical computer rather than considering he might be using drugs. Dilbert points out that denial and paranoia are classic symptoms, and Wally wonders if the Boss is high at that very moment.
punchline: The Boss's insistence that the tests must be rigged, rather than that he is on drugs, is itself the textbook behavior of a drug user.
summary: A manager shuts down a drug testing program after failing it himself, blaming sabotage and unwittingly displaying the very signs the test is meant to catch.

title: Attractive Date Shows Up Late

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: She's an hour late.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hi, Ellen. Didn't we agree on seven?

transcript.speaker: Ellen
transcript.text: Hi, Dilbert.

transcript.speaker: Ellen
transcript.text: I was ready on time but I decided to shampoo my carpets.

transcript.speaker: Ellen
transcript.text: Then I got involved in a crossword puzzle.

transcript.speaker: Ellen
transcript.text: This is how attractive people assert their superiority over the rest of you.

transcript.speaker: Ellen
transcript.text: Don't take it personally. I have a complete disregard for the feelings of all ugly people.

transcript.speaker: Ellen
transcript.text: I'll make this adorable face and you'll go into a stunned-ugly-guy stupor and forget the whole thing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh...what were we talking about?

transcript.speaker: Ellen
transcript.text: You were explaining why you didn't bring me any flowers.

setting: A restaurant table
situation: Dilbert waits at a restaurant table for his date Ellen, who arrives an hour late. She casually admits she was shampooing carpets and doing a crossword, then openly explains that attractive people use lateness to assert superiority. She announces she will make an adorable face to stun him into forgetting, and it works.
punchline: Ellen predicts she can manipulate Dilbert with her good looks, and he immediately falls for it, even letting her blame him for not bringing flowers.
summary: A tardy, good-looking date cheerfully admits her bad manners are a power play, then proves her point by flipping the blame onto her dazzled companion.

title: Pandering to the Boss's Major

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What's your presentation going to be about?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Rectangles. We heard the Boss was a geometry major.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Good thinking. But I heard he was a geography major, not geometry.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wyoming: one of the many rectangular states.

setting: Conference room during a meeting
situation: Dilbert tells a coworker that his presentation will be about rectangles, because he heard the Boss majored in geometry. The coworker points out that the Boss actually studied geography, so Dilbert hastily adapts his topic. He ends up presenting Wyoming as one of the many rectangular states.
punchline: Dilbert doesn't bother learning anything new for the presentation; he just awkwardly bolts his existing topic onto the Boss's real interest to flatter him.
summary: Preparing a pitch to please the Boss, Dilbert learns he guessed the wrong academic background and cheaply patches his rectangle talk with a map of Wyoming.
themes: tailoring the message to the audience

title: Breaking a Tie With a Baby

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The minutes from the last family meeting show that all the votes were a one-one tie.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: One of us will have to have a baby so we can break these ties.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I vote that you have the baby.

setting: Dilbert's home, at a table or desk
situation: Dilbert reads the minutes of the last family meeting and notes that every vote ended in a one-one tie between him and Dogbert. He proposes that one of them have a baby to supply a tiebreaking vote. Dogbert immediately casts a vote that Dilbert should be the one to have the baby.
punchline: Dogbert uses the very voting process under discussion to push the absurd burden of childbearing onto Dilbert, who cannot possibly comply.
summary: A two-member household committee deadlocks on every decision, and the proposed fix of adding a voter backfires when the dog votes for the human to produce one.

title: Experts Trample Their Own Crop Circle

transcript.speaker: Reporter
transcript.text: I'm standing at the Wickford wheat fields outside of London, the site of mysterious giant circles, possibly caused by aliens.

transcript.speaker: Reporter
transcript.text: How do you find these circles of crushed wheat?

transcript.speaker: Expert
transcript.text: My team of experts starts at one point and searches outward until . . .

transcript.speaker: Expert
transcript.text: Good Lord! Another circle has formed around us!!

setting: A wheat field outside London
situation: A news reporter interviews a crop circle expert about how his team locates the mysterious circles of crushed wheat. The expert explains that his team starts at one point and searches outward. In the last panel, his team is walking in a ring around him and he is amazed that a new circle has formed.
punchline: The experts are crushing the wheat themselves by walking outward in a circle, so they are creating the very crop circles they claim to be discovering.
summary: A scientist baffled by a fresh crop circle fails to notice that his own searching team has just trampled it into existence.

title: Mother Nature Punishes Butterfly Killers

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Look! A beautiful Regency butterfly!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Beautiful?? It's a flying bug.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It may not seem like much now...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But after we kill it, dip it in chemicals, and flatten it between glass, it becomes a beautiful work of art!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Do we throw away the bug guts and just keep the wings?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No. The guts keep the wings evenly spaced.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: EEOW!!! Ants in my pants!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Mother Nature!

transcript.speaker: Old Man
transcript.text: He was standing right on an anthill. I couldn't resist.

setting: Outdoors among green bushes and a dirt clearing
situation: Dilbert spots a butterfly and, while Dogbert calls it just a bug, describes how it could be killed, chemically treated and pressed between glass to make art. When Dilbert explains the guts keep the wings evenly spaced, he suddenly gets ants in his pants. Mother Nature, an old man with a staff, admits she put him on an anthill on purpose.
punchline: Dilbert's cheerful plan to kill and mount a butterfly earns him instant retribution from Mother Nature, who deliberately had him standing on an anthill.
summary: A man enthusing about turning a butterfly into a pinned display gets swarmed by ants courtesy of a vengeful personification of nature.

title: Dogbert Hosts Poltergeist Farm Documentary

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's World of the Unexplained

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm at the farm of Kay and Clem Bovinski...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: ...the location of unexplained phenomena.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: (Deep voice) The disturbances have lasted 40 years.

transcript.speaker: Kay
transcript.text: Objects move all by themselves. Sometimes they hit Clem.

transcript.speaker: Clem
transcript.text: I reckon it's poltergeist. No other explanation makes sense.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: BONK!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Cut.

setting: A rural farm and its farmhouse living room
situation: Dogbert hosts a paranormal TV documentary at a farm, interviewing a couple who say objects move by themselves and sometimes hit Clem. As Clem declares it must be a poltergeist, a lamp flies into his head. In the last panel it's revealed that Dogbert has been throwing the lamp himself, with Clem's feet sticking up from behind the couch.
punchline: The 'unexplained' phenomenon is actually staged by Dogbert, who ends the shoot by calling 'Cut' after hitting Clem with the lamp.
summary: A pseudo-documentary about a haunted farm turns out to be faked by the host, who flings household objects at a farmer for the cameras.

title: Presentation on Uses of Rectangles

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, put together a presentation for the big boss's staff meeting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: On what topic?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hear the big boss was a geometry major, so let's work that in somehow.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you do an hour on the many uses of rectangles?

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to prepare a presentation for the big boss's staff meeting but gives no topic. Having heard that the big boss majored in geometry, he decides the talk should somehow relate to that. He ends up asking Dilbert for a full hour on the many uses of rectangles.
punchline: The Boss picks a presentation topic purely to flatter the senior executive's college major, resulting in an absurd hour-long talk on rectangles with no real business purpose.
summary: Hoping to impress his superior, a manager assigns an employee a lengthy talk about rectangles based on a rumor about the executive's degree.

title: Philately Will Get You Nowhere

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Help me look for valuable stamps. You're better at this than I am.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Philately will get you nowhere.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: (No dialogue. Dilbert sits with stamps stuck all over his face and head.)

setting: A desk in Dilbert's office or home
situation: Dogbert, sitting on a desk with a magnifying glass and a scattering of small stamps, asks Dilbert to help him find valuable ones. Dilbert lectures that stamp collecting (philately) will get you nowhere. In the last panel, Dilbert is silent with stamps stuck all over his face and head, apparently from Dogbert.
punchline: Dilbert's pun-laden quip that philately 'will get you nowhere' is answered by Dogbert getting him literally covered in stamps, so he ends up the one stuck with them.
summary: A dog's request for help sorting through a pile of stamps leads to a corny pun and a face full of adhesive squares.

title: Dilbert's Cellmate and the Corn Lunch

transcript.speaker: Cellmate
transcript.text: What are you in for?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I killed a man with an ear of corn. But I was provoked.

transcript.speaker: Cellmate
transcript.text: Hey, look! Corn for lunch. Can you believe that?

setting: A jail cell
situation: Dilbert sits on a bench in a jail cell beside a large, bald, tattooed cellmate who asks what he is in for. Dilbert calmly admits he killed a man with an ear of corn, claiming he was provoked. When a lunch tray arrives, the cellmate cheerfully points out that corn is being served.
punchline: The cellmate, delighted by the coincidence of corn being served for lunch, is oblivious to the fact that the mild-mannered Dilbert has just confessed to killing someone with it, and the tough-looking inmate is the one acting innocent.
summary: A meek-looking man's startling confession of corn-based homicide is met by his cellmate's cheerful excitement over the lunch menu.

title: Dilbert's Staged Forehead Slap Backfires

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Forgot my keys.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll have to slap my forehead and mutter when I turn around, otherwise I'll look silly.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Too hard.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Smack

setting: Office hallway
situation: Dilbert walks down a corridor, realizes he forgot his keys, and thinks through how to act naturally in front of onlookers. He plans a theatrical forehead slap so he won't look silly when he turns around. He slaps himself so hard that he is knocked off his feet in front of a woman and a coworker, who watch.
punchline: In trying to avoid looking silly with a rehearsed gesture, Dilbert overdoes the slap, knocks himself off his feet, and looks far sillier than if he had simply turned around.
summary: A man carefully plans a casual self-slap to cover for a forgotten item, then clobbers himself in front of witnesses.

title: Dogbert Nominated to Supreme Court

transcript.speaker: Advisor
transcript.text: Mister President, there's another opening on the Supreme Court. One of the old guys wandered away.

transcript.speaker: Advisor
transcript.text: I recommend nominating a dog this time. They tend to be loyal and everybody likes them.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's for you... George Somebody.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Take a message.

setting: The Oval Office, then Dilbert's home
situation: An advisor tells the President that a Supreme Court seat has opened up because one of the elderly justices wandered off, and he recommends nominating a dog because dogs are loyal and well liked. In the last panel Dilbert hands a cordless phone to Dogbert, saying the call is from a George somebody, and Dogbert coolly tells him to take a message.
punchline: Dogbert, the dog the President is presumably nominating, is so self-important that he brushes off a call from the President (George Somebody) as if he were a nobody.
summary: A political aide suggests a canine for the high court, and the dog in question snubs the commander in chief's phone call.

title: The Awkward Hallway Eye Contact Dance

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now for the "Dance of the Eye Contact."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I pretend to look at spots on the wall. If our eyes meet too soon we'll have to awkwardly smile for ten seconds.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I hate the first smile of the day.

setting: Office hallway
situation: Dilbert walks down a hallway toward an approaching coworker and narrates in his thoughts his strategy for avoiding awkward eye contact. He pretends to study spots on the wall so their eyes don't meet too early. When he finally looks over, the coworker is thinking the exact same dread about the day's first forced smile.
punchline: Both people are going through the same silly avoidance ritual and dreading the same social awkwardness, so the awkwardness is mutual and unavoidable.
summary: Two coworkers passing in a corridor each privately fret over the strained courtesy of exchanging their first smile of the morning.

title: Boss Gloats Over Bigger Paycheck

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's pay day.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ha ha!! Dance for your paycheck!! Ha ha ha!! Mine is twice as big!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And they say money can't buy happiness.

setting: Office cubicle
situation: The Boss walks up to Dilbert's desk on pay day, waving a paycheck. He taunts Dilbert, telling him to dance for his paycheck and boasting that his own is twice as big. He then walks away, thinking to himself about the saying that money can't buy happiness.
punchline: The Boss's gleeful gloating over his larger salary ironically proves that money can indeed buy happiness, at least the smug kind that comes from lording it over subordinates.
summary: A gleeful manager taunts his employee with a fatter paycheck and then smugly decides that money buys joy after all.

title: Date Scored With Checklist Card

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: I'm using a new system for evaluating my dates. I just check off boxes on this card throughout the night.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: There... I just dinged you a point for that nervous twitch.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: Would you say your head is more like a block or a bucket?

setting: A restaurant table with a flower vase and wine glasses
situation: Dilbert is on a dinner date with a woman who explains she is rating him with a checklist card, ticking boxes as the evening goes on. She deducts a point for his nervous twitch, then asks him an awkward question about whether his head is shaped more like a block or a bucket, scoring him like a product inspection.
punchline: The date treats Dilbert like an item being evaluated against a quality checklist, and the absurd head-shape question shows how superficial and insulting her scoring criteria are.
summary: A woman grades her dinner companion with a scorecard, docking points for his nerves and then quizzing him about the shape of his skull.

title: Random Drug Testing Blood Loophole

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Starting today, the company will begin random drug testing.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Although it would be illegal to search your car or home for illegal drugs . . .

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: We have found no ethical problem with sucking the blood out of your body.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Results will be posted in the cafeteria.

setting: Office
situation: A manager announces the company will begin random drug testing while Dilbert and a coworker listen. He notes that searching employees' cars or homes would be illegal, but says the company sees no ethical problem with drawing their blood. He adds that the results will be posted publicly in the cafeteria.
punchline: Management's ethics are absurdly selective: searching your car is off-limits, but extracting your blood is fine, and the results will be publicly displayed with no regard for privacy.
summary: A manager cheerfully explains that the firm's new drug screening takes blood instead of searching property, then promises to publish everyone's results for all to see.

title: Dilbert Pays Dogbert to Pet Him

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ten dollars... It's my final offer.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Okay, but you can only use one hand.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Pat pat

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't believe this is now standard in the dog industry.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Oh, right, I suppose the others give it away.

setting: Dogbert's desk, with Dilbert leaning over it
situation: Dilbert haggles and offers Dogbert ten dollars, and Dogbert agrees on the condition that Dilbert may only use one hand. Dilbert pats Dogbert on the head while paying him. Dilbert then complains that this is not standard in the dog industry, and Dogbert replies sarcastically.
punchline: Dogbert is charging for something other dogs give away free, the petting, and mocks Dilbert's complaint by quipping that the others just give it away.
summary: A man pays a dog for the privilege of petting him, only to protest that the going rate for canine affection is supposed to be zero.

title: Android Built From A Kit

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I built this android from a kit.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He doesn't have a personality, but he will walk around and talk.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Well, I hope you guys will at least dress differently.

setting: Dilbert's home or lab
situation: Dilbert shows Dogbert the android he assembled from a kit, tinkering with a screwdriver as the bald figure sits with its head open. He explains the android has no personality but can walk and talk. Dogbert dryly responds by hoping the two of them will at least dress differently.
punchline: Dogbert implies that Dilbert is so personality-free and bland that he is indistinguishable from a personality-less android, so they would need different clothes to be told apart.
summary: Dilbert proudly presents a homemade robot with no personality, and Dogbert slyly suggests the machine and its creator are practically identical.

title: Blind Date With Dog Woman

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is absolutely the LAST blind date.

transcript.speaker: Dog Woman
transcript.text: ...Then I realized...

transcript.speaker: Dog Woman
transcript.text: I'm a woman trapped in a dog's body... So, now I'm saving for a species change operation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it expensive?

transcript.speaker: Dog Woman
transcript.text: Well, you can imagine the electrolysis costs alone...

setting: A restaurant table during a dinner date
situation: Dilbert sits at a restaurant on a blind date, privately vowing it will be his last. His date, who looks like a dog in a dress, explains that she is a woman trapped in a dog's body and is saving for a species change operation. Dilbert politely asks if it is expensive, and she mentions the electrolysis costs.
punchline: Dilbert's date is literally a dog who identifies as a woman, and her matter-of-fact worry about the cost of removing all that fur with electrolysis shows how absurd the blind date has become.
summary: A man's hopeless blind date turns out to be a canine who believes she is a woman in the wrong body and is budgeting for the transformation.

title: Sneeze Causes Executive Toupee Disaster

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How was work?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Not so good... I sneezed and blew the toupee off a vice president's head and into the face of the director of marketing, who fell and broke a rib.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Gesundheit.

setting: Dilbert's home, after work
situation: Dilbert comes home carrying his briefcase and Dogbert asks how work went. Dilbert explains that his sneeze blew a vice president's toupee into the director of marketing's face, causing the director to fall and break a rib. Dogbert responds only with a single word.
punchline: Dogbert ignores the injuries and chaos entirely and offers the polite but wildly inadequate response of 'Gesundheit' to the sneeze.
summary: A man's sneeze at the office sets off a chain of embarrassment and injury, and his dog's reply barely acknowledges any of it.

title: New CEO Learns Leadership Is Luck

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now that I'm CEO, what am I supposed to actually do?

transcript.speaker: Advisor
transcript.text: You're supposed to make superficial statements about how good the company is, then hope something lucky happens and profits go up.

transcript.speaker: Advisor
transcript.text: It's called leadership, sir.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Make it so.

setting: CEO's office
situation: Dilbert, newly promoted to CEO and sitting in a big leather chair, asks a suited advisor what the job actually involves. The advisor explains that a CEO just makes vague, upbeat statements and hopes for good luck to raise profits. Dilbert, pleased, adopts the role and says 'Make it so.'
punchline: The job of CEO is reduced to empty cheerleading and hoping for luck, which the advisor cynically labels 'leadership.'
summary: A freshly minted chief executive discovers from his aide that running a company mostly means saying nice things and crossing his fingers.

transcript.text: Guys who know wine.

situation: Bob the Dinosaur, a destructive green dinosaur, rips the pants off various types of men the narrator dislikes: a smug cyclist in a helmet, a showy dancer, and a pretentious wine connoisseur. Each victim is mocked with a pun by Bob. In the last panel, Dilbert is revealed as a guy who kills a conversation with a nerdy remark, and Bob's hand reaches in for him next.
punchline: Dilbert's conversation-stopping comment about trellis code modulation marks him as one of the annoying guys who deserves to have his pants ripped off.
summary: A pants-stealing dinosaur targets irritating show-offs, and the final victim turns out to be the strip's own engineer hero.

title: Self-Service Gas Attendant School

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Dogbert's School for Self-Service Gas Station Attendants will not be easy.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Phillips! What would you do if a customer couldn't figure out how to use the pumps?

transcript.speaker: Phillips
transcript.text: Nothing. It's self-service.

transcript.speaker: Another student
transcript.text: Great...there goes the curve.

setting: A classroom at Dogbert's training school for gas station attendants
situation: Dogbert, acting as a teacher, warns a class of uniformed gas station attendants that his school will be demanding. He quizzes a student named Phillips about helping a customer who can't work the pumps, and Phillips answers that you do nothing because the station is self-service. Another student, thinking to himself, laments that Phillips's correct answer ruins the grading curve.
punchline: The test question is so trivially easy that the student's obvious answer (do nothing) is correct, undermining Dogbert's claim that the school will be hard and making a classmate worry about the grading curve.
summary: A dog running a school for pump attendants asks a trick question whose answer is that attendants do nothing, which leaves a classmate fretting about grades.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert

transcript.text: This movie line is too long.

transcript.text: Hunh!

setting: Dilbert's living room, then a daydream outside a movie theater
situation: Dilbert sits watching a violent TV show while Dogbert muses that a karate chop to knock someone out would be useful in real life. Dogbert daydreams about standing in a long movie line and karate-chopping the people ahead of him one by one. He ends up at the ticket window, pleased with himself.
punchline: Dogbert's fantasy of solving a long line by knocking out everyone ahead of him ends with him smugly noting that no one else has used that tactic, which is why he gets to the front.
summary: Inspired by television action, Dogbert imagines chopping his way past an entire movie queue and gloats that he is the only one ruthless enough to try it.

title: Dilbert's Meaning of Life: Electricity

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Would the world be any worse off if I'd never been born?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wait... If not for me, who would turn off this computer every night. I'm saving electricity!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I found meaning in my life today.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You left your bedroom light on all day.

setting: Dilbert's cubicle at work, then arriving home
situation: Dilbert sits at his computer and gloomily wonders whether the world would be worse off if he had never been born. He decides his life has meaning because he turns off his computer every night, saving electricity. At home he proudly announces this to Dogbert, who points out he left his bedroom light on all day.
punchline: Dilbert's grand claim to a meaningful existence is undercut by Dogbert noting he wastes more electricity than he saves, so his life's meaning is effectively cancelled out.
summary: A despondent engineer convinces himself he matters because he saves power, only for his dog to reveal he wastes it elsewhere.

title: Elbonian Mud Luggage Hunting

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dilbert lands in Elbonia without his suitcase.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian Servant

transcript.speaker: Elbonian Lord
transcript.text: I like to think this helps maintain the delicate balance of nature.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian Servant
transcript.text: Yes, sire.

setting: Elbonia, a muddy swamp-like landscape
situation: Dilbert arrives in Elbonia and plunges headfirst into the mud, while his suitcase is missing. Two Elbonians then appear, and the lord shoots Dilbert's suitcase as if it were a wild animal, dragging it through the mud. He pompously claims that hunting luggage keeps nature in balance.
punchline: The Elbonians treat a stray suitcase like big-game prey and justify the hunt with pious talk about ecological balance, while Dilbert remains stuck headfirst in the mud.
summary: In a backward muddy land, a nobleman proudly hunts a traveler's lost baggage like trophy game.

title: Dogbert Critiques Dilbert's Smelly Book

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well? What do you think of my book so far?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It reminds me of "Moby Dick."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because of my creative metaphors and strong imagery?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No, it just seems to me that a big whale wouldn't smell too good, either.

situation: Dogbert lies in bed while tall-hatted, bearded Elbonians tend to him, explaining that their country forgot its religious ways during forty years of communism. One Elbonian says Dogbert's fall from the sky was a sign from... and can't recall the name of the deity. Another supplies 'Doug,' and they all cheer for Doug, with Dogbert now the object of worship.

summary: Forgetful Elbonians who lost their faith under communism improvise a deity's name and start worshipping the dog who dropped from the sky.

setting: Office break area
situation: Alice is sitting in the office with her newborn baby, who was born at work, while Dilbert and Wally sit nearby. The Boss suggests she should name the baby after him. Alice calmly replies that she already did, then addresses the baby with an insulting name while offering more milk.

summary: A self-flattering manager angles for the honor of a newborn's namesake and gets quietly insulted by the mother instead.

title: Dogbert's Guilt Lecture Pays Regardless

situation: Dogbert stands on a stage holding a microphone and introduces himself as the presenter of a lecture series on coping with guilt. He promises the audience they will learn his method within the hour. He then admits that if they don't learn anything, he still gets paid.
punchline: Dogbert's cheerful admission that he is paid whether or not the audience benefits shows he has no accountability for results, which is a guilt-free attitude of its own.
summary: A self-help speaker promises to teach his audience to handle guilt, then casually reveals his paycheck doesn't depend on whether it works.

title: Dogbert Watches TV, Plans Conquest

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Those people are idiots. They should all drive over here and proclaim me their king.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The secret to happiness is high expectations and your own bag of chips.

setting: A room with a TV (off-panel), where Dogbert sits on a cushion
situation: Dogbert sits alone on a cushion watching television and thinks about how foolish the people on screen are. He decides they should all come and crown him their king. In the last panel he settles in with a bag of chips and shares his formula for happiness.
punchline: Dogbert's formula for happiness is absurdly grandiose, combining delusions of world domination with the simple comfort of snack food.
summary: Watching TV convinces a smug Dogbert that he deserves to rule the world, and he settles for happiness with a bag of snacks while he waits.

situation: A police officer with a gun shows up at Dilbert's door, accusing him of staying up late playing with his computer instead of going to sleep. Dilbert says he simply wasn't tired. The officer then pats him down against the wall with his hands up as if arresting him.
punchline: The officer turns the criminal charge 'resisting arrest' into a pun, claiming Dilbert was 'resisting a rest' because he refused to go to bed.
summary: A cop arrests a computer-loving engineer for the crime of not going to bed on time, capped with a wordplay on resisting arrest.

summary: A cynical montage mocks public spending by showing silly gadgets, scary lessons, baffling art, a microwaved patient and lawmakers congratulating themselves on their raises.

situation: Dogbert approaches Dilbert, who is working at his computer, and announces he has solved an ancient puzzle: how many angels can dance on the head of a pin. Dilbert gives no reply, and in the last panel Dogbert walks off thinking that whatever Dilbert thinks, the answer is six.
punchline: Dogbert confidently declares a precise answer to a famously unanswerable philosophical question, and defiantly insists on it regardless of any objection, with no reasoning or evidence offered.

summary: A self-styled prophet defends a hopelessly vague doomsday forecast by dressing it up in financial jargon.

summary: A get-rich-quick publishing scheme by a dog yields a tiny reference book that is mostly self-promotion with a laughably thin nod to a whole country.

situation: Dilbert sits at his computer and tells Dogbert that knowledge is power, predicting that computer-literate people will one day rule over those who aren't. He adds that the rulers will have a special name for people like him. Dogbert deadpans that the name is 'secretaries'.
punchline: Dogbert points out that people who actually operate computers are not rulers but low-status support staff, undercutting Dilbert's optimistic belief that technical skill brings power.
summary: A hopeful prediction about computer experts inheriting authority is deflated by a dry reminder of how workplaces really treat people who do the typing.

setting: A series of vignettes in streets, a road, a bar or event hall, and public places
situation: The strip is a list of tactics women might use to avoid Dilbert, with each panel illustrating a tactic and Dilbert's oblivious reaction. He chases a jogger, waves at a woman hiding behind her hair, and misses every hint, such as talk of a boyfriend, a fake number, and an all-male ladies' night.
punchline: Dilbert is so socially clueless that he fails to notice every obvious rejection tactic, even interpreting them as mysteries or taking them at face value.
summary: A mock instruction manual lists the lengths women go to dodge a hopelessly awkward man who never catches on.

title: Mud Flaps and Second Thoughts

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: With these on my car, women will think I'm a sexist Neanderthal, and men will be embarrassed to share my gender.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But now I'm having second thoughts.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That implies you had first thoughts.

setting: Dilbert's home
situation: Dilbert holds up a pair of mud flaps decorated with the silhouette of a naked woman and explains that he bought them. He then realises they will make women think he is sexist and make men embarrassed to share his gender, so he is reconsidering. Dogbert, lounging nearby, mocks him for having had any thought before the purchase.
punchline: Dogbert points out that having 'second thoughts' implies Dilbert had first thoughts, insulting his judgment in buying the mud flaps without thinking.
summary: After buying tasteless mud flaps, a man belatedly foresees how badly they'll reflect on him, and his dog quips that he never thought it through in the first place.

title: Dilbert's Dusting Creates Giant Cloud

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Did your mother teach you to dust that way?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We didn't call her the "Grey Fox" because of her clever brownie recipe.

setting: Dilbert's home living room
situation: Dilbert announces he will dust and zips around the room flicking a feather duster at the furniture, lamp and picture frame. Instead of removing dust, he stirs up clouds that grow until they fill the whole room. Dogbert then asks if his mother taught him to dust that way, and Dilbert replies with an odd remark about her nickname.
punchline: Dilbert's mother was nicknamed the "Grey Fox" because of her hair, not her baking, which suggests she was an attractive older woman and makes his answer an awkward and unexpected non sequitur.
summary: A man's feather-dusting spree only fills his home with ever-larger dust clouds, and when his dog quizzes him about his technique he oddly defends his mother's attractive nickname.

title: Rat Disguised as Tiny Kangaroo

situation: Ratbert sits on a chair and confides in Dogbert, who listens silently like a therapist. Ratbert explains that he once tried to escape the stigma of being a rat by painting a pouch on his belly and pretending to be a tiny kangaroo. He concludes that people hate tiny kangaroos too.
punchline: Ratbert's disguise failed because the prejudice wasn't about being a rat in particular; people simply dislike small, unwelcome creatures, so changing his appearance did nothing.
summary: A rat recounts his failed attempt to dodge public disdain by faking a marsupial pouch, only to discover the disguise earned the same contempt.

punchline: Ratbert hints at a lesson about prejudice, but Dogbert misses the point entirely and concludes that Chihuahuas must actually be evil.
summary: A bruised, disguised Ratbert hopes to teach a moral about bigotry, but his companion draws the opposite conclusion.

When Rex relays his dad's heart-and-gut version of morality, Dogbert mocks the dad's tiny brain, and Rex ends up agreeing.
punchline: Dogbert's cynical definition of morality is delivered alongside an insult that Rex's dad has such a small brain that his organs do the thinking, and Rex cheerfully piles on.
summary: A small dinosaur seeks moral guidance from a sarcastic dog, who offers a self-serving definition and then ridicules the dinosaur's gut-driven father.

situation: Dilbert sits on a green couch holding hands with a date and offers her a romantic compliment about her eyes. He then follows it with a horrifically unflattering comparison of her lips to earthworms. He returns home early, where Dogbert asks about it and Dilbert notes he at least avoided kissing the worms.
punchline: Dilbert's attempt at romantic flattery collapses into an insulting simile, ending the date early, and he comforts himself that he escaped kissing her 'worm' lips.
summary: A man's smooth compliments turn into a grotesque insult that cuts his date short, leaving him with a bitter consolation.

setting: Dilbert's front doorway
situation: A police officer arrives at Dilbert's door with a drawn gun and arrests him for killing a senior executive of his company with an ear of corn. Dilbert protests that it was self-defense during a food fight and that he reflexively used the corn he had just seasoned. The officer responds by stating the charge as a pun on 'assault and battery with intent to kill'.
punchline: The officer's formal charge, 'a salt and buttering with intent to kill', is a pun on 'assault and battery' that treats Dilbert's seasoning of the corn as part of the crime.
summary: A cop busts Dilbert for an extremely unusual office killing and sums up the charge with a condiment-flavored legal pun.

title: Dilbert's Car Is Buried in Dirt

situation: Dogbert, sitting on the front steps, advises Dilbert to wash his car as Dilbert arrives home with his briefcase. Dilbert admits it's easy to get used to the car being dirty. The final panel reveals the car is completely caked in a huge mound of dirt, with plants and a bird's nest growing on it.
punchline: Dilbert has neglected the car for so long that it looks like a overgrown hill of dirt with a nest on top, yet he only mentions it's slightly hurting his gas mileage, a huge understatement.
summary: A man who has let his car go unwashed for ages calmly blames the grime for a minor fuel-economy dip, while the vehicle is literally a soil-covered mound hosting a bird.

title: Dinosaur's Petition Has No Complaints

punchline: A petition with no grievance, just a dim-witted "D-uhh," gets signed anyway, which Dogbert sarcastically hails as democracy at work.
summary: A dim dinosaur collects signatures for a petition that protests nothing, and Dogbert cheerfully signs it, mocking the political process.

title: Teenager Spirals Into War With Norway

punchline: Dogbert dismisses the teenager's absurd, escalating fears and then piles a trivial new worry on top by shouting about a pimple attack.
summary: A fretful kid catastrophizes his way from deforestation to military conscription, and Dogbert tops it off with a cruel acne scare.

title: Dogbert Pays Rich Man to Wallow

situation: Dogbert, thinking happily about being rich, spots a wealthy man in a suit walking past. He offers the man ten thousand dollars to wallow in a mud puddle, and the man promptly does so, ending up face-down in the mud in his suit.
punchline: Dogbert is amused that a rich man will humiliate himself in the mud for a sum he doesn't need, then sarcastically wonders how rich people ever get bored when they can simply pay for entertainment like this.
summary: After daydreaming about wealth, Dogbert amuses himself by paying a well-dressed rich man to roll around in the mud.

title: Dilbert Asks Dinosaur Bob How

situation: Dilbert muses aloud to Bob, a dinosaur coworker, about how someone with such a tiny brain manages to survive, and asks how he does it. Bob responds by visibly straining to think of an answer, so Dilbert hastily withdraws the question.
punchline: Dilbert's insult backfires because Bob takes the question seriously and visibly strains to answer, proving Dilbert's point about his tiny brain and making Dilbert regret asking.
summary: After mocking a dinosaur coworker's small brain, Dilbert watches him labor over a reply and quickly drops the matter.

punchline: Because the government can't afford to repay depositors, it gives them the S&L owner's purchases, and Dogbert's share is a corrupt senator, implying the owner bought politicians with the missing money.
summary: A bankrupt government pays off swindled savers with the crook's leftover purchases, and Dogbert's prize turns out to be a bought politician.

punchline: The Elbonians' idea of fundamental rights is a list of silly, trivial freedoms, which the advisor excuses as merely a first draft.

punchline: The android's gloating about immortality collapses almost immediately, since living forever means little when you're bored within moments, implying eternity would be tedious.
summary: A gloating android boasts of eternal life, then promptly admits that being alive forever already has him bored.

situation: Dogbert announces he is opening a vocational school and says it will train self-service gas station attendants. Dilbert points out that this means charging students to learn how to sit and do nothing. Dogbert replies that it's surprising no one has already started such a business.

summary: Dogbert plans a trade school whose graduates will be paid to do absolutely nothing at gas stations where customers pump their own fuel.

summary: A consultant hired at a steep hourly rate polls the staff and returns with a verdict that pins every problem on the man who hired him.

situation: A top executive invites Dilbert to lunch, claiming he wants to learn what the workers think and encouraging him to speak freely. summary: A boss-level lunch meant to hear honest worker feedback ends with the diner threatening to pelt the honest employee with a side dish.

situation: Dilbert finishes presenting a simple proposal to the Executive Committee and asks for questions. punchline: Dilbert's presentation was so dull and ridiculous that the executives ignored the content and mocked his delivery, and even Dogbert joins in the ridicule at the end.
summary: After a presentation nobody listened to, the committee amuses itself by lampooning the presenter's performance, a mockery that extends all the way to his own dog.

Their flying saucer fires a beam down at Earth, which hits Dilbert sitting in his armchair watching television. He is left smoking and singed, with his clothes tattered and his hair frazzled, as a warning not to investigate Stonehenge either.
punchline: The aliens' warning shot to protect their secret crop-circle landing sites lands on a random, innocent TV viewer, Dilbert, who gets blasted and threatened with no idea why.
summary: Extraterrestrials guarding their secret landing sites vaporize the nearest human, who is just trying to watch TV.

title: Poor Dilbert's Fancy Salad Dressing

situation: Dilbert sits on a bench next to Dogbert and complains about how poor he used to be, claiming he could only afford two-bean salad. Dogbert says that sounds awful, and Dilbert admits it wasn't so bad. He then reveals he always covered it in hundred island dressing, undercutting his claim of poverty.
punchline: Dilbert's tale of hardship collapses when he admits he lavishly smothered his cheap salad in hundred island dressing, a fancier version of thousand island, so he wasn't really that poor.
summary: A man recalling his impoverished diet of bean salad undermines his own sob story by confessing to a luxurious condiment habit.

title: Mandatory Categories in Comedy Competition

setting: Dilbert's home living room
situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert he plans to enter a stand-up comedy competition and reads aloud from the rules sheet. After a single minute of freestyle, the remaining four minutes are dictated by required joke topics.
punchline: The competition's 'mandatory categories' are the most tired, cliched comedy subjects imaginable, so the contest forces every comic to use worn-out material for most of their set.
summary: A would-be comedian reads the contest rules and discovers that nearly all of his stage time is reserved for predictable, stale joke topics.

title: Dogbert's Fake Berlin Wall Museum

transcript.speaker: Elderly Man

setting: Dogbert's museum, with a display pedestal
situation: Dogbert, acting as a museum curator, shows an elderly couple a supposedly authentic chunk of the Berlin Wall on a pedestal. The woman points out that the rock exactly matches a hole in his sidewalk. Dogbert claims he traded sidewalk for the Berlin piece, and the husband makes his wife apologize.
punchline: Dogbert's absurd explanation that he swapped a piece of his sidewalk with Berlin is accepted by the gullible husband, showing how easily people believe a confident con artist.
summary: A scheming dog passes off a chunk of his own sidewalk as a historic relic and talks his way out of being caught.

title: Executive Claims To Be Normal, Smarter

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: And of course, I'm much, much smarter.

setting: Restaurant table during a lunch with an executive
situation: Dilbert sits quietly at lunch while an off-panel executive tries to assure him that he is just a regular guy. He admits to a higher salary and a nice office, then tacks on that he is far smarter than Dilbert. Dilbert says nothing throughout.
punchline: The executive's attempt at humble relatability collapses into condescending arrogance, revealing he believes his rank reflects superior intelligence.
summary: A boss-level lunch host insists he is an ordinary person, then steadily lists every way he considers himself better than his guest.

title: Dung Beetle Powers Mean Politics

situation: Dilbert sits in a blue superhero costume with a cape, waiting to see whether a bite from a radioactive dung beetle has given him any super powers. The narrator wonders what powers a dung-dwelling bug could confer. Dogbert asks if he feels anything, and Dilbert says he only feels an urge to enter politics.
punchline: The only power Dilbert gains from the dung beetle is a desire to go into politics, implying that politicians are full of dung.
summary: A superhero-costumed Dilbert awaits powers from a radioactive dung beetle bite and ends up craving a political career.

title: Blindfolded Dart Staff Cuts

punchline: The Boss's random, reckless approach to layoffs literally kills an employee, and he proudly dismisses the tragedy as a sign of decisive management.
summary: A manager picks who gets laid off by hurling a dart blindfolded, hits a coworker instead of a chart, and boasts about his decisiveness.

title: Dogbert's Upside-Down Stamp Scheme

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: Dogbert excitedly tells Dilbert he has found a valuable stamp that was misprinted upside down. Dilbert examines it and points out that Dogbert was simply holding it the wrong way up. Dogbert walks away, privately admitting the attempt to get rich was worth trying.
punchline: Dogbert's get-rich-quick claim collapses because he merely held the stamp upside down, and he shrugs off the failed ploy as a gamble worth taking.
summary: A dog hopes a misprinted collectible has made him wealthy, only for his friend to reveal the mistake was entirely his own grip.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Not today-- we have a staff meeting.

setting: Dilbert's office and the engineering department
situation: Dilbert lectures Zimbu, a monkey who learned language at the zoo, saying that engineering takes more than language skills. When Wally invites them to get donuts, Dilbert happily revises his claim, and Wally mentions a staff meeting while they all eat donuts at the desk.
punchline: Dilbert's supposed engineering standards collapse at the mention of free donuts, and it turns out the only real qualifications for the job are showing up in the morning and eating pastry.
summary: A skeptical engineer lectures his simian coworker on what makes a real engineer, then drops the argument the moment donuts and slacking off are on offer.

The customer then sits in the car, proud of his bargaining, and Dogbert reveals it is the car he drove to the lot.
punchline: The customer, proud of his negotiating skills, has unknowingly just bought his own car from Dogbert, who tricked him into paying for what he already owned.
summary: A proud haggler beats a salesman down on price, only to learn he has purchased the very car he arrived in.

title: Elves' Magic Trick Backfires Badly

situation: A group of green-hatted elves try to intimidate Dogbert by announcing they are magic and performing a trick with a top hat. The trick produces an enormous angry bunny that scares the elves and makes one of them, Karl, eat a bug. The surviving elves later reflect that they had Dogbert's respect right up until that moment.
punchline: The elves' attempt to look powerful and intimidating falls apart when their own magic trick produces a bunny that humiliates them, destroying the fear and respect they were trying to earn.
summary: Tiny magical elves try to awe a dog with a hat trick, but the huge rabbit they conjure bullies them instead and ruins their reputation.

title: Dogbert Plots While Dilbert Misjudges

summary: While his owner assumes he is mindlessly idle, a dog quietly weighs up the best way to subjugate mankind.

summary: A man who traded his top job for a calmer one learns that relaxation is a luxury his new salary won't cover.

punchline: Dilbert's sewing skill, inherited from his mother, includes the family habit of accidentally stitching oneself to the furniture.
summary: A man proudly credits his mother for his sewing skills, then reveals both of them tended to fasten themselves to the couch.

punchline: Dogbert turns an engineer's absorption in his computer into a carnival attraction, profiting from the fact that he won't notice being pelted with balls.
summary: A scheming dog charges museum guests to pelt a focused programmer with soft balls while he stares at his screen, completely unaware.

situation: Dilbert, seated at his computer, asks Dogbert about the closure of his school for self-service gas station attendants. punchline: Refolding a road map is so maddening that it supposedly drove an entire class of trainees to their deaths, delivered as a deadpan reveal.
summary: A dog explains that his training academy folded after a map-folding lesson ended in total casualties.

summary: A defense attorney dog summons a trash collector as an all-knowing legal expert, who reveals a bizarre old corn law that Dogbert immediately seems eager to exploit.

situation: Dilbert asks his boss what he meant by announcing that all employees are empowered. He hopefully lists the freedoms it might bring, such as controlling his own budget, skipping layers of approval and taking calculated risks. The boss deflates him by explaining that empowerment is only a device for blaming employees when they don't do things they were told not to do.
punchline: "Empowerment" gives employees no real authority; it is a new buzzword invented to shift blame onto them, which Dilbert sarcastically notes is why a new word was needed.
summary: A hopeful employee learns that being 'empowered' carries all the accountability and none of the actual authority.

summary: A patient who got a rushed, careless checkup and a bill learns that complaining will get him nowhere.

punchline: The missile is literally 'smart' and makes boring small talk about PBS while 'boring in' on Dogbert, a pun on a smart weapon and a boring conversationalist.
summary: A would-be dictator in a flying saucer is chased down by a chatty missile whose dull small talk doubles as its attack.

situation: Dilbert sits at his computer and solemnly describes becoming one with the machine, calling it a blissful blend of logic and emotion. As he declares he has reached some higher state, Dogbert, sitting at the bottom of the frame, supplies the word "Nerdvana."

summary: A computer enthusiast describes a transcendent union with his machine until his dog finishes the thought with a nerdy pun on nirvana.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's time to end this charade, Zimbu!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your language skills are simple rote behavior. Monkeys are incapable of logic and reasoning.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ha! And that program you're writing -- it's probably in "BASIC."

transcript.speaker: Zimbu
transcript.text: Do you ever work?

setting: Office cubicle with a computer
situation: Dilbert confronts Zimbu, a monkey who works as a programmer, claiming his language skills are just rote mimicry and that monkeys cannot reason. He leans over the monkey's shoulder to mock the program he's writing as probably being in BASIC. Zimbu calmly turns the tables by asking whether Dilbert ever does any work himself.
punchline: While Dilbert is busy trying to expose the monkey as a fraud, the monkey is the one actually working, so the monkey's question exposes Dilbert's own unproductiveness.
summary: A smug engineer tries to debunk his simian colleague's abilities and gets shown up by a simple question about his own work ethic.

title: Sick Excuse for Missing Doctor

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I missed my doctor's appointment. Can I reschedule it?

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Why did you miss it?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I was sick.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Yeah, like I haven't heard that one before.

setting: Doctor's office reception desk
situation: Dilbert approaches the receptionist at a doctor's office and asks to reschedule an appointment he missed. When she asks why he missed it, he says he was sick. She sarcastically dismisses the excuse as one she hears all the time.
punchline: Dilbert's perfectly legitimate excuse, being sick, is the one reason a doctor's office should accept, yet the jaded receptionist treats it as a tired lie.
summary: A man gives the most obvious and reasonable excuse for skipping a medical appointment, only to be met with a bored receptionist's cynicism.

situation: Dogbert visits an image consultant, explaining that he wants to become a pop psychologist and needs help making a lecture video. The consultant, a woman in sunglasses behind a desk, offers him a new look. Dogbert then appears on a platform wearing a blonde wig and a cone-shaped bra, and the consultant dismisses the outfit.
punchline: Dogbert's makeover copies Madonna's famous cone-bra stage costume, and the consultant deadpans that even Madonna's version of the look didn't work very well.
summary: A dog hoping to launch a career as a self-help guru gets styled in a pop star's infamous costume and is told it was never a winner.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Rrrrr

situation: Dilbert struggles to open a jar of spaghetti sauce while cooking. Dogbert offers to humiliate him by opening it easily, but fails too, so he hands it to Bob the dinosaur, who smashes the jar and covers himself in sauce. Dilbert then irritably asks the sauce-covered Bob to stop humming.
punchline: Bob the dinosaur, boasting he is mighty, smashes the jar over his own head and, covered in sauce, cheerfully hums Sinatra's "My Way" as if he succeeded his own way.
summary: A stubborn jar defeats a cook and his dog, and the muscle brought in as a last resort wrecks it with messy, tuneful confidence.

title: Dinosaur Eagerly Accepts Flunky Job

transcript.speaker: Bob

situation: Dogbert, newly rich, offers Bob the dinosaur a job as his flunky. Bob is thrilled and says he has always dreamed of being one. He immediately starts licking the windows clean with his tongue while Dogbert looks on.
punchline: Dogbert sarcastically remarks that the work ethic isn't dead as Bob eagerly volunteers for a degrading servile job, licking windows clean.
summary: A newly wealthy Dogbert hires an overjoyed dinosaur as his servant, who happily begins cleaning the glass with his tongue.

title: Blind Date With A Dog

transcript.speaker: Judy

setting: A blind date, apparently at a restaurant or similar spot, against a plain blue background
situation: Dilbert sits across from his blind date, Judy, who turns out to be a dog in a dress. He tactlessly tells her he wouldn't have come if he had known she was 'a woman trapped in a dog's body'. Judy, unimpressed, fires back by predicting his brush-off line about being friends and petting her.
punchline: The insult Dilbert thinks is a clever way to let her down is turned on him, as Judy sarcastically points out that the friend-zone speech would involve petting her like a pet, since she is literally a dog.
summary: A man politely rejects his blind date for having a canine body, and she sarcastically beats him to the awkward let-her-down speech.

punchline: Dogbert, the despotic ruler of Elbonia, is using the airborne Dilbert as skeet-shooting target practice, since arrivals by slingshot look like clay pigeons.
summary: A traveler flung into a backward country by slingshot discovers the tyrant he seeks is already taking aim at him for sport.

title: Tobacco Lobbyist Smokes Her Own Head

transcript.text: What we need is more attention on the positive aspects of smoking ... like sex appeal.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yes, sir.

setting: Lobbyist's smoke-filled office
situation: A tobacco lobbyist, her head completely engulfed in a cloud of cigarette smoke, meets with Dogbert and a senator who has a 'SALE' sign on his head. She offers to buy the senator, complains about anti-smoking fascists and the media, and says smoking needs better PR around its sex appeal. By the last panel the smoke has thinned to reveal her ragged, unhealthy-looking face, and Dogbert dryly agrees.
punchline: The lobbyist argues for smoking's sex appeal while visibly looking haggard and half-suffocated by her own smoke, and Dogbert's flat 'Yes, sir' shows how absurd her claim is.
summary: A smoke-shrouded tobacco lobbyist tries to buy a senator and plug smoking's glamour, undermined by her own wrecked appearance.

situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert, who is lounging in a chair, that he feels judged by everyone he meets. As he asks why people can't accept others without judging them, Dogbert responds by holding up a scorecard reading 7.5 and critiquing the delivery of his speech.
punchline: Dilbert's complaint about being judged is immediately answered by Dogbert judging it like a figure-skating or talent-show performance, proving his point ironically.
